lines.text: A real car has size, a rope stretches a little, and a wheel has friction. A useful mechanics model keeps the properties that affect the question. Which of these details can you ignore in a particular calculation?

A particle has mass but negligible dimensions. A lamina is a flat sheet of negligible thickness. A rigid body does not change shape or size under the forces considered. A light rod or string has negligible mass, light does not mean unable to transmit force. A uniform rod has mass evenly distributed along its length and, in uniform gravity, its centre of mass is at the midpoint. A non uniform rod has uneven mass distribution. An inextensible string keeps a constant length when taut, so connected particles have linked displacements. A smooth surface has no friction but can exert a normal reaction, a rough surface may exert friction. A light smooth pulley has negligible mass and no friction at the string contact, with a light string, tension is equal on both sides. A bead is a small object constrained to move along a wire. A wire defines its path, a peg is a fixed small support around which a string can pass. A peg or wire needs a stated smoothness assumption before friction is ignored.

In a later connected particle problem, first use inextensibility to link motion, then use the light string and smooth pulley to link tensions. For a rod in a moments problem, uniformity determines where its weight acts, rigidity only tells you its shape stays fixed.

Particle, mass retained, size negligible, lamina, negligible thickness, rigid body, no deformation. Light, negligible mass, uniform, evenly distributed mass, non uniform, uneven mass distribution. Inextensible, constant taut length, smooth, no friction, rough, friction may act. Light smooth pulley with light string, equal tensions on both sides. Bead, small object constrained to a wire, peg, fixed support for a string.
A uniform rod rests on a smooth table. Which assumption places its weight at the midpoint, and which removes friction? Explain why the table can still exert a normal reaction.

A light inextensible string passes over a smooth pulley. Which conclusion follows from the model? The string has no tension because it is light. The taut string keeps a constant length and can carry tension. The string cannot move because it is inextensible. The pulley cannot exert any contact force because it is smooth. B Light means negligible string mass, while inextensible means constant length when taut. Smooth removes friction at contact, not tension or the contact force.
State what is meant by treating a body as a particle.
The body retains its mass, its size and shape have no effect on the motion being modelled.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
State what is meant by a lamina.
A thin flat sheet whose thickness is negligible compared with its other dimensions.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
State what is meant by a rigid body.
Its shape and size do not change under the forces considered.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Find the property represented by a light rod.
Light means negligible mass, so the rod can still transmit force. Equal mass distribution describes a uniform rod.
Focus on what the model simplifies.
Separate mass, size, and deformation.
Check which physical property the adjective describes.
State the difference between a uniform rod and a non uniform rod.
A uniform rod has constant mass per unit length, so its centre of mass is at its midpoint. A non uniform rod need not have its centre of mass there.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
State the two assumptions for a light inextensible string.
Light removes the string's own weight from the model. Inextensible means it does not stretch, tension may still be present.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Find the force that a smooth horizontal table can exert on a resting block.
Smooth means frictionless contact. The table can still exert a normal reaction on the block.
Focus on what the model simplifies.
Separate mass, size, and deformation.
Check which physical property the adjective describes.
State what a rough surface permits that a smooth surface does not.
Rough contact can exert friction, its size depends on the situation. Smooth contact has no friction.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
State the assumptions of a light smooth pulley.
The pulley's mass and bearing friction are neglected. With a light string, the tension is the same on both sides of a smooth pulley.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Find what inextensibility implies for two particles joined by a taut string over a fixed pulley.
The total taut string length is fixed, so one end moving a given distance makes the other end move the same distance along the string. The particles can move and may have different masses.
Focus on what the model simplifies.
Separate mass, size, and deformation.
Check which physical property the adjective describes.
State what is meant by a bead moving on a wire.
A bead is modelled as a small object threaded on a wire, its path is constrained by the wire. Contact friction depends on whether the wire is specified as smooth.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Explain how a peg differs from a pulley in a string model.
A peg is fixed and a pulley rotates. A peg must be specified as smooth before friction can be neglected.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Explain why a uniform rigid rod can have a non zero weight even if its shape does not change.
Rigid and uniform describe different properties. A uniform rod may be heavy, its centre of mass is at the midpoint.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Explain the modelling assumptions needed to use equal tension on both sides of a pulley in a connected particle problem.
For a light string passing over a smooth pulley, tension is equal on the two sides. Light alone does not remove pulley friction.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
Explain whether a rough wire guarantees friction acts on a stationary bead, and give a reason.
Rough means friction is available. If there is no tendency to slip along the wire, the friction force can be zero.
Identify which property of the model matters.
Connect the stated assumption to a physical quantity.
Write the implication in the context of the object.
A car is driven along a straight road. Explain why the car can be modelled as a particle when finding the time for the journey, but not when investigating the turning of its wheels.

Modelling as a particle neglects dimensions, not mass, along a straight road only the position of one point matters, so the journey time is unaffected. Rotation is a property of an extended body, so a point with no size cannot represent a spinning wheel, a rigid body model is needed instead.
Decide which property of the car the particle model throws away, and which it keeps.
Compare the size of the car with the length of the journey.
Ask what a single point with no dimensions is unable to do.

A small metal ring slides along a fixed straight horizontal wire. The ring is modelled as a bead and the wire is modelled as smooth. Explain what each of these two assumptions means for the forces on the ring and for its motion.

Bead removes the ring's size and fixes it on the wire, so its motion is one dimensional along the wire. Smooth removes only the tangential friction, the wire still pushes on the ring with a normal reaction perpendicular to it, which is what supports the ring's weight.
Take the two words one at a time and name the property each one neglects.
Decide in which direction the contact force can act once friction is removed.
Ask what holds the ring up if there is no friction along the wire.
A diving board is fixed at one end and is modelled as a uniform rigid rod. Find the statement that follows from this model.

Uniform means the mass is evenly distributed, so the weight acts at the midpoint, and rigid means the board keeps its shape under the forces. Uniform and rigid say nothing about how much mass there is, about friction at the support, or about the board's length, a rod keeps its length.
Translate each of the two words in the model into one consequence.
Check whether each statement is about mass distribution, amount of mass, friction or size.
A rod model keeps one dimension, its length.
one Mathematical models in mechanics.
In one breath.

A mechanical model keeps the properties needed to answer a question and simplifies the rest. Read each adjective literally, it tells you which effect may be ignored and which forces or motions remain possible.
Key ideas.

A particle has mass, but its dimensions are negligible for the question. Treat a car as a particle when finding its motion along a road, its shape is irrelevant to that calculation. A lamina is a flat sheet whose thickness is negligible compared with its other dimensions. A rigid body keeps its shape and size under the forces being considered. It can still move, rotate and have weight.

A rod is a thin straight body. A light rod has negligible mass, so its own weight can be ignored, but it can still transmit a force. In a uniform rod, mass is evenly distributed along its length, in a uniform gravitational field its centre of mass is at the midpoint. A non uniform rod has uneven mass distribution, so you cannot assume that midpoint result. Light, uniform and rigid describe different properties. A rod may be uniform and rigid without being light.

A light string has negligible mass. An inextensible string keeps a constant length when taut, although it can move. If two particles are joined by a taut inextensible string over a fixed pulley, their displacement magnitudes along the string are equal. The string can still have tension, in the usual ideal model it pulls but does not push.

A smooth surface is frictionless, but can exert a normal reaction. A rough surface may exert friction tangential to the contact, depending on whether slipping tends to occur. Rough does not imply that the friction force is always non zero. A light smooth pulley has negligible mass and no friction at the string contact. For a light string over it, the tension is the same on either side. Its rotation changes the string's direction without changing that tension in the ideal model.

A bead is a small object threaded on a wire and constrained to move along the wire. A peg is a fixed small support around which a string can pass, unlike a pulley, it does not rotate as a wheel. Friction at a wire or peg can only be neglected when smoothness is stated or justified.
Method.
Name the actual object and the model used for it, for example, a cyclist as a particle or a bar as a rigid rod.
Translate each modelling word into a consequence. Light removes the object's own mass, smooth removes friction, inextensible fixes length. Do not remove other forces.
Use the consequence in the equation or explanation. For instance, equal displacements in equal times give equal speed magnitudes for particles linked by a taut inextensible string.
Check the model's limits, size matters for rotation, mass distribution matters for moments, and friction may matter at rough contact.
Worked example.

Two particles are joined by a light inextensible string passing over a fixed light smooth pulley. One particle moves down by zero point two zero metres. Explain the other particle's motion and compare the tensions. The taut string's total length is constant, so the segment on the other side must shorten by zero point two zero metres. The other particle moves up by zero point two zero metres. The string is light and the pulley is smooth, so its tension has the same magnitude on both sides. Neither assumption says that the tension is zero.
Traps.
Trap, A particle has no mass. Why it's wrong, Only its dimensions are neglected. Instead, Keep its mass in force and momentum calculations.
Trap, Smooth contact supplies no force. Why it's wrong, Smooth means no friction. Instead, Keep the normal reaction, or the string tension at a smooth pulley.
Trap, An inextensible string cannot move. Why it's wrong, Its length stays constant while its parts can move. Instead, Relate the motions of the connected objects.
Trap, Uniform means light. Why it's wrong, Evenly distributed mass can be substantial. Instead, Decide separately whether mass is negligible and whether it is evenly distributed.
Exam technique.

For State, give the assumption precisely, such as negligible mass or no friction. For Explain, link that assumption to a concrete consequence, the string is inextensible, so the two particles have equal displacement magnitudes along it. Do not claim equal tension around a peg unless its contact is specified as smooth. If a rod is non uniform, do not place its weight at the midpoint without further information.
